clue.text: Islam and law reviewed in Camp David?

indicators.note: to review something is to go over it again, here reworking the order of the letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
joins the two words of fodder

explanation.surface: Religious and legal matters under scrutiny at the US presidential retreat in Maryland.
explanation.walkthrough: Camp David is the US president's country retreat, but here 'camp' is an adjective: David Walliams is a British comedian known for flamboyant, camp characters in Little Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The comic actor and children's author David Walliams is famous for theatrical, exaggerated camp performances on British television.

clue.text: Rubbish violin part heard on the radio

indicators.note: radio is a medium of sound only, so the word is identified by how it is spoken

parts.note: the narrow middle of a violin's body is its waist

explanation.surface: A critic on the radio dismisses a violin passage as junk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Violin part' suggests a musical part to be played, but it is a physical part of the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Waste is refuse, discarded material, which is the noun sense of rubbish.

clue.text: Criminal certain to nick shilling after pound?

definitions.text: Criminal certain to nick shilling after pound?

indicators.note: places the rest of the construction behind the piece for pound

parts.note: L, from Latin libra, is the pound sign

indicators.note: nicking means taking something and keeping it inside, so one piece is held within another
something criminal is crooked or bent out of shape, so the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters are taken as written
s is the abbreviation for the old shilling coin

explanation.surface: A crook who is sure to steal small change after a bigger sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' does double duty: it signals the anagram and, with the rest, describes the thief. A shilling was a pre-1971 British coin worth a twentieth of a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: A larcenist is someone who commits larceny, the legal term for theft, so a thief certain to steal.

clue.text: Long letter needing its introduction cut

indicators.note: cutting an introduction removes the opening, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: the spelt-out name of the letter H

explanation.surface: A lengthy piece of correspondence that needs its opening trimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective describing the letter but is the verb, to yearn; the letter is H, spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: To itch for something is to yearn or crave it impatiently, the verb sense of long.

clue.text: One likely to ruin married line manager?

parts.note: the abbreviation for married
an angler manages a fishing line

explanation.surface: Questioning whether a wedded office boss is someone who wrecks things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line manager' looks like an office boss, but here it is someone who handles a fishing line.
explanation.definitionFit: A mangler is someone who mutilates or botches things, so a person who tends to spoil or wreck.

clue.text: Totally knackered after winning result

indicators.note: says the piece for the first words follows the piece for winning, fixing their order

parts.note: a team that is up is ahead, winning
British slang: shot means worn out, ruined

explanation.surface: An exhausted player still manages a victory in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Knackered is British slang for exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: An upshot is the final outcome or consequence of events, the same thing as a result.

clue.text: Sanction how mercenaries might be paid

definitions.meaning: second meaning, split as two words

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning only works when the answer is split into the Latin-style 'per' plus 'mission'.
explanation.definitionFit: Permission is formal consent or authorisation, which is the noun sense of sanction.

clue.text: High-definition screens popular with one foreign-language speaker

indicators.note: with adds the final piece alongside the rest
a screen shields what is behind it, so the outer piece encloses another

parts.note: the standard abbreviation for high definition
something in is fashionable, popular
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: High-definition television screens are a hit with a viewer from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screens' looks like TV displays but is the verb, to hide behind. Hindi can name a person who speaks the language as well as the language itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Hindi, the main language of northern India, also serves as a noun for someone who speaks that tongue.

clue.text: Sex brought about visible inflammation and fatigue

indicators.note: bringing something about turns it round, so the word is read the other way

parts.note: it is a coy word for sex
inflamed skin shows as red

explanation.surface: Intercourse led to a rash and exhaustion.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiredness is the state of being weary and needing rest, which is the noun sense of fatigue.

clue.text: A thought entertained

parts.note: taken as written
to muse is to ponder, so mused means thought

explanation.surface: An idea someone considered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entertained' looks like 'considered', as in entertaining a thought, but it means delighted.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone amused has been diverted and made to smile, the past participle sense of entertained.

clue.text: Hospital screening career rugby player?

indicators.note: to screen something is to hide it behind a cover, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: short for sanatorium
to career is to rush along, to race

explanation.surface: A hospital hiding away someone's whole working life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' looks like a noun meaning profession but is the verb, to hurtle. Saracens are a London rugby union club.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Saracens club in English rugby union could be called a Saracen, hence the question mark.

clue.text: One in a fleet entering foreign sea?

definitions.text: One in a fleet entering foreign sea?

indicators.note: the word for one is placed inside the following pieces
going into something means ending up enclosed by it

parts.note: French for sea
the Royal Navy, Britain's fleet
Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A naval vessel sailing out into waters abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: RN, the Royal Navy, is a standard crossword fleet; read as a whole, the clue also describes a sailor setting off overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: A mariner is a sailor, exactly the kind of crew member found aboard the ships of a navy heading out to sea.

clue.text: Sheep? There are two in Nauru, I'm told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: the name Nauru contains two of the letter U

explanation.surface: Someone claims the Pacific island of Nauru has only a couple of sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural of the letter U, said out loud, is the same as the plural of a female sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewes are female sheep, so the plural answer stands for a flock of the animals.

clue.text: As CID files, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests one arrangement among several, so the letters can be put in another order

parts.note: the letters are taken as written

explanation.surface: Describing how police detective records might be kept.
explanation.walkthrough: The CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, Britain's plain-clothes police detectives; their files would be secret, so the whole clue also defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Police investigation records would be marked secret and restricted, which is what classified documents are.

clue.text: Tall building editor evacuated after dogfight?

indicators.note: puts the piece for editor behind the piece for dogfight

parts.note: a dogfight is an aerial battle, a scrap in the sky

indicators.note: evacuating a word clears out its middle, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of editor

explanation.surface: A tower's editor fled once a fight between planes broke out.
explanation.walkthrough: A dogfight is a close air battle between fighter planes; scrap is British slang for a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A skyscraper is a very high multi-storey building, the archetypal tall structure of a city.

clue.text: Where kids struggled with mutton chops?

indicators.note: things that struggle are thrown about in disorder, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters are taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking where children had trouble eating a lamb dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Mutton chops look like meat on a plate but are bushy sideburns.
explanation.definitionFit: Mutton chops are long side whiskers, so someone sporting them has facial hair on the cheeks.

clue.text: Drunk, but not making a squeak?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: a hinge that has been thoroughly lubricated is silent

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a quiet drunk; the second meaning is the literal machinery sense of the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-oiled is an informal idiom for being fairly drunk, and literally describes smoothly lubricated machinery.

clue.text: Material from kids brought round in hearing

indicators.note: within hearing means as spoken out loud, so only the sound counts

parts.note: someone brought round to a view has been persuaded, swayed

explanation.surface: Fabric from children won over by argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kids' are young goats, not children: suede is often made from kidskin.
explanation.definitionFit: Suede is soft leather with a napped surface, traditionally made from the skin of young goats.

clue.text: Take out china after priest comes round at home

indicators.note: places the friend's piece behind the priest's piece

parts.note: Eli is the priest in the Book of Samuel, a crossword regular

indicators.note: coming round something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: Cockney rhyming slang: china plate means mate
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Collecting porcelain after a clergyman pays a house visit.
explanation.walkthrough: China is Cockney rhyming slang (china plate), so it means a friend rather than porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: To eliminate someone is to remove or kill them, and take out is an idiom for both.

clue.text: A great deal to secure you a fast car

indicators.note: securing something means holding it in, so one piece is kept inside another

parts.note: lots means a great deal
text-speak spelling of you

explanation.surface: A bargain that would land you a sports car.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotus is a British maker of sports cars, so one of its models is a fast car.

clue.text: Nothing about May's party works

parts.note: short for 'sweet FA', slang for nothing at all
c, circa, means about
Theresa May led the Conservatives, the Tories

explanation.surface: A complaint that the Conservative government under Theresa May achieves nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' looks like a verb but is the plural noun for industrial plants.
explanation.definitionFit: A works is a factory or industrial site, so the plural noun names manufacturing plants.

clue.text: Addict knocking back bar's last Bud

indicators.note: knocking back a drink means taking it in, so one piece is swallowed by another

parts.note: a fiend is an addict, as in dope fiend

indicators.note: last points to the final letter of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter of bar

explanation.surface: A drinker downing the last Budweiser at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bud' looks like the beer, but it is short for buddy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bud is American slang for buddy, a friend or pal.

clue.text: Drug a German injected into Morse?

indicators.note: something injected goes inside, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: Morse is a code of dots and dashes
German for a

explanation.surface: Inspector Morse is given a shot of something by a German.
explanation.walkthrough: Morse suggests the fictional Oxford detective, but here it is the signalling code.
explanation.definitionFit: Codeine is an opiate painkiller derived from morphine, a medicinal drug.

clue.text: Writer Mark Reckless found in empty office

indicators.note: something found in a place is located inside it
emptying a word leaves just its two end letters as a shell to hold other pieces

parts.note: the outer letters of office
a scar is a mark left on the skin
wild means reckless, uncontrolled

explanation.surface: A writer finds that the politician Mark Reckless has turned up in a vacant office.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Reckless is a real British politician, so the name looks like a person rather than two words of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde was the Irish playwright and novelist behind The Importance of Being Earnest and Dorian Gray.

clue.text: Wire prisons about son receiving time

indicators.note: receiving something means taking it in, so the outer pieces hold another

parts.note: c, circa, means about
the abbreviation for son
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A news item on jails holding someone's boy for a long sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wire' looks like a verb, as in sending a telegram, but it describes what the prisons are made of.
explanation.definitionFit: Cages are enclosures of wire or bars that confine animals, so they are literally prisons of wire.

clue.text: Derisive noise that man's trousers initially smothered

indicators.note: trousers is read as a verb, to pocket, so one piece is slipped inside another

parts.note: belonging to that man

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the next word

parts.note: first letter of smothered

explanation.surface: A jeering sound muffled by someone's trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like a noun but is the verb to pocket; S goes inside HIS before its final S.
explanation.definitionFit: Audiences hiss to show scorn, so the sound is one of contempt or mockery.

clue.text: Old statesman unhappy thanks to U-turn

parts.note: sad means unhappy

indicators.note: a U-turn heads back the way it came, so the word is read from right to left

parts.note: British informal word for thanks

explanation.surface: An elderly politician is miserable about a policy reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Anwar Sadat was President of Egypt in the 1970s, a Nobel peace laureate assassinated in 1981.

clue.text: Strike the centre of gong for dinner?

indicators.note: to strike something out is to delete it, here its middle letter

parts.note: British slang: a gong is a medal or honour

explanation.surface: Hit the middle of the gong to call everyone to dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' suggests hitting a dinner gong, but it means cross out; a gong is British slang for a medal.
explanation.definitionFit: Dinner is one example of a meal, which the question mark signals.

clue.text: It might make a ball break off three stumps!

definitions.text: It might make a ball break

wordplay.note: stumps and pins are both slang for legs: a pair of legs plus a single pin make three

explanation.surface: A cricket delivery that bowls the off stump and all three come down.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface hides the slang: stumps, pins and legs are all words for the limbs, so two plus one is three. In cricket a ball breaks when it turns off the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Leg spin is a style of slow bowling in cricket where wrist action makes the delivery turn sharply after bouncing.

clue.text: Country shop that sold knackered horses?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Nordic island nation
second meaning: the British frozen-food supermarket chain caught up in the 2013 horsemeat scandal

explanation.walkthrough: Iceland is a UK frozen-food chain whose burgers were found to contain horsemeat in 2013; a knacker's yard slaughters worn-out horses.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the North Atlantic island republic and to a British frozen-food retailer.

clue.text: Long for wage rise director holds back

indicators.note: back says the held letters are read from right to left
the run of words holds the answer within them, spanning the word breaks

parts.note: the letters run across the end of wage, all of rise and the start of director

explanation.surface: Wanting the pay increase that a company boss is withholding.
explanation.definitionFit: To desire something is to crave or yearn after it, the verb sense of long for.

clue.text: Utterly determined underworld criminal

parts.note: the underworld of the dead
British slang: bent means corrupt or criminal

explanation.surface: A gangster from the criminal underworld who will stop at nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hell-bent on something is recklessly resolved to do it whatever the cost.
